prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: FAA NextGen aims to raise National Airspace System (NAS) capacity; en route weather causes ~70% of US delays. System: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3), ground/aircraft decision aids for weather-avoidance routing, TMI response, en route/arrival metering. Subset: NASA Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), cruise phase, using existing weather/airspace/traffic data and ATM automation. Current system: FAA traffic managers set static Flow Constrained Areas (FCA) and Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP, aka Playbook routes) 2-8 h ahead; airline flight dispatchers file flight plans >=45 min before push-back; Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) strategic only; controllers, dispatchers, flight crews request amendments manually; crews use flight management systems and limited-range on-board weather radar. Gap: no automation flags expired constraints or savings. DWR: ground-based automation continuously analyzing in-flight aircraft at/above 10,000 ft, updating with new radar track and flight plan data; seeks time/fuel-saving corrections to weather-avoidance or wind-favorable direct-to routes, considering convective weather, traffic conflicts, sector congestion, Special Use Airspace (SUA), FAA restrictions. Logic: reference direct route from Maneuver Start Point (MSP; default 5 min ahead) to Return Capture Fix (RCF; downstream fix on current Center route where correction rejoins flight plan). Default RCF set by a Center-unique limit function so direct route is operationally acceptable absent weather; depends on Center airspace, arrival routing limits, possibly city-pair routing and first-tier adjacent Center; generally not last fix in current Center. Fort Worth Center (ZFW) uses limit rectangle ~200 nmi beyond ZFW boundary. If wind-corrected savings >= user minimum (default 5 min), route probed; on weather conflict 1-2 auxiliary waypoints inserted (fix-radial-distance points); optional snap-to named fix replaces them for voice operations; weather (optionally traffic) free solutions meeting threshold posted to DWR alert list on user display. Current and advised trajectories checked for congested sectors and SUA; status shown in UI. Clicking advisory opens interactive trial planning to modify RCF, MSP, waypoints; savings and conflict status must update within 1 s; UI must strongly warn of conflicts. DWR extends NASA Direct-To tool; constraints modeled as polygons.

New part:
U0077: The default RCF is either the last flight plan fix inside the limit rectangle or, for aircraft landing inside the limit rectangle, the last fix before the arrival STAR.
U0078: Another approach is to analyze historically observed direct route clearances in each Center and use frequently occurring direct route clearances to define a convex limit polygon.
U0079: In this approach the limit polygon replaces the simpler limit rectangle, but the fix selection logic is otherwise the same.
U0080: This empirically derived limit polygon approach has been implemented in the Future ATM Concept Evaluation Tool (FACET) implementation of DWR called National Airspace System Constraint Evaluation and Notification Tool (NASCENT).
U0081: Other methods, such as choosing the RCF based on the particular city pair routing within a Center, could also be implemented.
U0082: Figure 3: Capture Fix Limit Regions (rectangle and polygon) Early in the testing of DWR at American Airlines, users identified the need for an MSP in the DWR trajectory modeling.
U0083: Depending on workload and other factors, users may need several minutes of coordination time before the point at which a flight is expected to depart the current trajectory to fly a DWR route.
U0084: An MSP located a user-definable number of minutes downstream of present position on the current flight plan trajectory, or for climbing flights, the point at which the flight is predicted to be in high-altitude airspace (FL240 for ZFW), enables users to see the effect of coordination delay on trajectory status parameters like weather proximity, flying time savings, traffic conflicts, and level flight status, which is particularly important for climbing flights that may not have reached the high altitude airspace.
U0085: Five minutes was generally the accepted default value used during the trials with American Airlines [3].
U0086: All DWR advisories initially incorporate the default MSP.
U0087: Once in trial planning, the user may adjust the MSP using click and drag inputs and assess the effect on status parameters.
U0088: If the MSP is within 10 nmi of a flight plan fix, the MSP snaps to the flight plan fix.
U0089: Auxiliary waypoints are added when needed to avoid weather, or optionally weather and traffic, and provide the minimum-delay route based on geometry and winds.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
